children: Chief Executive Scott Kirby defended rising airfares and additional charges for preferred seats, arguing that airlines must generate enough revenue to cover operating costs while giving passengers the option to pay more for amenities.

In an interview with The New York Times, Kirby said ticket prices have increased this year partly because of higher fuel costs associated with the war in Iran. He also argued that airfares remain below their 2019 levels after adjusting for inflation, despite a 22% year-over-year increase in September.

Kirby characterized the industry's pricing environment as a recovery from unusually low fares during the Covid-19 pandemic. He pointed to Spirit Airlines' shutdown and predicted that four of the eight publicly traded U.S. airlines would report losses this year, underscoring the financial pressures facing carriers.

For investors, Kirby's comments highlight United's strategy of protecting profitability through higher fares, premium seating and additional fees rather than competing primarily on price. The approach could support revenue and margins, particularly if reduced industry capacity gives airlines greater pricing power. However, sustained fare increases also risk weakening demand among cost-conscious travelers, especially if fuel prices remain elevated.
